question.text: At the same instant, two bodies, A and B, travel along a straight path in an identical direction. Particle A has an initial speed of 3 m/s and maintains a constant acceleration of 1 m/s², while particle B has an initial speed of 1 m/s and an acceleration of 2 m/s². If particle A begins at a position 10 m behind particle B, determine the closest distance of approach between the two particles.
conditions: motion along a straight line in the same direction
constant acceleration of A is 1 m/s²
constant acceleration of B is 2 m/s²
initial speed of A is 3 m/s
initial speed of B is 1 m/s
initial separation is 10 m with A behind B

solution.approach: Write the separation between B and A as a function of time and minimize it with calculus.

steps.text: Write each particle's position from its own start, then the separation as B's position minus A's position, starting from the given 10 m gap.
Set the derivative of the separation to zero to find the time of closest approach.
Substitute t = 2 s back into the separation to get the minimum distance.
steps.why_this_step: The second derivative of s(t) is positive, so this turning point is a minimum, not a maximum.

common_mistakes.text: Using only the initial speeds and ignoring the accelerations suggests the gap keeps closing forever, missing that B's larger acceleration makes B faster than A after t = 2 s, so the gap widens again.
